title: Standard Precautions: Treat Exposure Risk Every Time
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Standard Precautions apply to every patient. Match hand hygiene and PPE to the anticipated exposure rather than waiting for a known infection label.
recognize: Blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, nonintact skin, contaminated equipment, and respiratory secretions create exposure risk.
priorities: Perform hand hygiene and select gloves, gown, mask, and eye protection based on the task and expected exposure.
assessMonitor: Check PPE availability, isolation signage, exposure events, and adherence to hand hygiene.
interventions: Use safe injection, respiratory hygiene, environmental cleaning, and sharps practices.
medicationSafety: Never reuse single-dose medication containers or contaminated medication-preparation equipment between patients.
redFlags: Break in sterile or injection practice
teaching: Explain that hand hygiene and PPE protect both patients and staff.
delegationScope: All team members follow infection-control precautions; licensed nurses remain responsible for recognizing and escalating breaches affecting patient safety.
examTrap: Using Standard Precautions only for patients known to have infection.
oneLinePearl: Standard Precautions start before the diagnosis.

title: Contact Precautions: Stop Hands and Equipment From Carrying Pathogens
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Contact Precautions reduce spread by direct touch and contaminated surfaces/equipment. Use the facility's required gown/glove and dedicated-equipment workflow in addition to Standard Precautions.
recognize: Uncontrolled drainage, certain multidrug-resistant organisms, and selected enteric/skin infections may trigger Contact Precautions.
priorities: Follow posted PPE and room-entry requirements and dedicate or disinfect equipment between patients.
assessMonitor: Monitor skin/wound containment, room supplies, equipment movement, and PPE adherence.
interventions: Limit unnecessary transport and contain infected or colonized sites during required transport.
medicationSafety: Keep medication-preparation areas and clean supplies separate from contaminated bedside equipment.
teaching: Teach visitors the required hand hygiene and PPE process.
delegationScope: PPE tasks may be performed by all trained staff; the nurse escalates isolation failures and changing infection-control needs.
examTrap: Carrying a shared stethoscope to the next patient without disinfection.
oneLinePearl: Contact spread rides on hands and equipment.

title: Droplet Precautions: Protect the Face at Close Range
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Droplet Precautions add source-control and mask protection for pathogens spread primarily by respiratory droplets. Follow current facility/CDC pathogen-specific PPE requirements.
recognize: Coughing, sneezing, suctioning, and close respiratory care increase exposure risk.
priorities: Apply required mask/PPE before close contact and place a mask on the patient for transport when tolerated and indicated.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory symptoms, room placement, transport needs, and PPE compliance.
interventions: Use respiratory hygiene and minimize unnecessary exposure.
medicationSafety: Do not bring multidose medication supplies into contaminated zones unless policy permits and safe handling is assured.
redFlags: Aerosol-generating procedure without required respiratory protection
teaching: Teach cough etiquette and mask use as appropriate.
delegationScope: All staff follow posted precautions; aerosol-generating procedures may require additional competency/PPE.
examTrap: Assuming a surgical mask is automatically sufficient for every respiratory procedure.
oneLinePearl: Droplet care changes when the procedure creates aerosols.

title: Airborne Precautions: Respirator and Airflow Matter
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Airborne pathogens require respiratory protection and appropriate airborne-infection isolation controls. A routine surgical mask on staff is not an adequate substitute for required respirator protection.
recognize: Suspected or confirmed airborne infections require immediate isolation workflow while diagnosis is being clarified.
priorities: Use the designated airborne room when required and wear fit-tested respiratory protection according to policy.
assessMonitor: Verify room/door requirements, respirator use, patient transport necessity, and exposure events.
interventions: Limit transport and apply patient source control during essential transport as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Coordinate time-sensitive medication administration without unnecessary room entries while preserving safe verification.
redFlags: Airborne-risk patient in an uncontrolled shared space
teaching: Explain why room airflow and respirator use are part of treatment safety.
delegationScope: Respirator use requires training/fit testing; staff should not enter when required protection is unavailable.
examTrap: Entering an airborne-isolation room with only a standard surgical mask.
oneLinePearl: Airborne safety is respirator plus environment—not one or the other.

title: C. difficile Precautions: Soap, Water, and Environmental Control
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Suspected or confirmed C. difficile requires prompt enteric/contact control, appropriate hand hygiene, and sporicidal environmental cleaning. Diarrhea after antibiotic exposure is a cue to escalate, not merely treat symptomatically.
recognize: New frequent watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, recent antibiotics, or healthcare exposure raise concern.
priorities: Initiate facility enteric/contact precautions promptly when indicated and notify the RN/provider for testing/treatment decisions.
assessMonitor: Track stool frequency, hydration, abdominal findings, vital signs, renal function/labs as ordered, and signs of severe colitis.
interventions: Use dedicated equipment and required sporicidal cleaning; follow CDC/facility hand-hygiene workflow.
medicationSafety: Avoid reflexive antidiarrheal treatment without clinical review when infectious colitis is possible.
teaching: Complete prescribed therapy and use careful hand/environmental hygiene at home.
delegationScope: Stool output may be recorded by assistive staff; licensed nurses interpret deterioration and escalate.
examTrap: Giving an antidiarrheal first and ignoring recent antibiotic exposure.
oneLinePearl: New antibiotic-associated diarrhea is an infection-control problem until proven otherwise.

title: Device Infection Prevention: Remove the Unneeded Route
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Urinary catheters, vascular lines, and other invasive devices create infection risk for as long as they remain in place. Question ongoing necessity and protect every access/manipulation with the required aseptic technique.
recognize: Fever, drainage, erythema, tenderness, cloudy urine, unexplained sepsis, or line malfunction may indicate device-related infection depending on context.
priorities: Assess device necessity and site/system integrity and escalate suspected infection.
assessMonitor: Track indication, insertion/site findings, closed-system integrity, duration, and infection cues.
interventions: Maintain closed systems, disinfect access points, secure devices, and remove promptly when ordered/no longer indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not use a potentially infected or malfunctioning access route for medications without clinical review when an alternative is needed.
teaching: Patients should avoid unnecessary handling and report pain, drainage, fever, or device dislodgement.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; necessity assessment and infection escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Keeping an invasive device because it is convenient for staff.
oneLinePearl: The safest unnecessary device is the one that comes out.

title: Needlestick Exposure: Wash, Report, Evaluate Now
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: A sharps or mucous-membrane exposure is time-sensitive. Perform immediate first aid, report through the occupational-exposure pathway, and obtain prompt source/exposed-worker evaluation for indicated post-exposure management.
recognize: Percutaneous injury, blood splash to mucosa, or blood contact with nonintact skin can create occupational exposure.
priorities: Wash needlestick/cut sites with soap and water; flush exposed mucous membranes; report immediately.
assessMonitor: Document exposure type, source information when available, vaccination status, and follow-up testing plan.
interventions: Use occupational health/emergency evaluation promptly because some prophylaxis is time-sensitive.
medicationSafety: Do not self-start, borrow, or delay indicated post-exposure prophylaxis while waiting for symptoms.
teaching: Follow the complete testing and prophylaxis schedule even when initially asymptomatic.
delegationScope: Exposure reporting is the exposed worker's immediate responsibility; evaluation follows institutional protocol.
examTrap: Squeezing or aggressively scrubbing a puncture wound instead of washing and reporting promptly.
oneLinePearl: First aid now, report now, evaluate now.

title: Clean vs Sterile Technique: Match the Procedure, Do Not Improvise
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Aseptic requirements depend on the procedure and setting. When sterile technique is required, contamination means the field/item is no longer sterile and must be corrected rather than rationalized.
recognize: Touching a sterile item with a nonsterile object, moisture strike-through, an out-of-view field, or uncertain sterility can contaminate a sterile setup.
priorities: Know whether the procedure requires clean or sterile technique before starting and gather supplies first.
assessMonitor: Watch field integrity, hand position, package integrity, expiration, and environmental contamination.
interventions: Replace contaminated supplies/field and restart the affected step safely.
medicationSafety: Use aseptic medication preparation and injection technique; never compromise sterility to avoid wasting supplies.
teaching: Home wound-care technique should match the prescribed clean/sterile plan and available supplies.
delegationScope: Procedure performance depends on competency and policy; the person performing it is responsible for maintaining required technique.
examTrap: Continuing because the contaminated item only touched the edge briefly.
oneLinePearl: If sterile status is uncertain, treat it as contaminated.

title: Immunocompromised Patient: Small Infection Cues Can Be Big
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients may deteriorate with subtle or atypical infection findings. Fever, chills, new respiratory/GI symptoms, line changes, or sudden weakness require prompt evaluation based on the patient's treatment plan.
recognize: Neutropenia, transplant immunosuppression, biologic therapy, chemotherapy, and high-dose immunosuppression can blunt inflammatory responses.
priorities: Follow the patient's fever/infection action plan and escalate promptly rather than waiting for classic purulence or marked leukocytosis.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, hemodynamics, respiratory status, line/wound sites, CBC/ANC when ordered, and new symptoms.
interventions: Use meticulous hand hygiene, food/environment precautions as prescribed, and rapid sepsis evaluation when indicated.
medicationSafety: Immunosuppressants and biologics have drug-specific hold/infection rules; do not generalize one medication's rule to another.
redFlags: Fever meeting the treatment plan threshold
teaching: Patients should know exactly what temperature/symptoms trigger same-day or emergency contact.
delegationScope: Routine temperature collection may be delegated; interpretation and escalation require licensed judgment.
